means:
Giving **sparingly**, holding back, rationing out less than is wanted or deserved. To **stint** on something is to skimp on it; to **stint** someone is to keep them short.

This isn't thrift you admire — it's withholding something that ought to have flowed freely: praise, effort, food, money, time. A budget airline is *economical*; a host who serves one sandwich to twelve guests is **stinting**. Note where you'll actually meet it: nine times out of ten in the negative — *without stinting*, *never stinted*, **unstinting** support. So when the bare positive form shows up on the exam, read it as grudging rationing.
trick_line: **Stint** and **stunt** are the same word wearing different vowels — both cut something short before it reaches full size.
trick_unpack: A stunted tree never got its full growth; a stinting host never gave you your full share.
sentences: The committee was **unstinting** in its praise, devoting three full pages to her contribution.
Don't **stint** on the garlic — nobody's ever complained about too much.
in_the_wild: You already use the noun: *"I did a two-year **stint** at Deloitte."* A stint is a rationed, measured-out spell of time — the same idea of a portion cut to size.
etymology: Old English **styntan** = *"to blunt, to make dull, to cut short."* Blunt it → shorten it → give less of it. The same root surfaces as **stunt** (to check something's growth), which is why the two feel related — they are.
one_line: Sparing, grudging — giving less than is due.
root: Old English styntan (to blunt, cut short)
